title: Bagtech (June 2013 FCA) Federal Court of Appeal Case
subject: Unanimous Shareholder Agreement and De Jure Control of a CCPC
summary: In Canada v. Bioartificial Gel Technologies (Bagtech) Inc., 2013 FCA 164, the Federal Court of Appeal held that director-election clauses in a Unanimous Shareholder Agreement under the CBCA count in the de jure control test, so a corporation with over 60% non-resident shareholders kept its Canadian-controlled private corporation status and its entitlement to refundable 35% SR&ED investment tax credits.
metaDescription: Learn about the June 2013 Federal Court of Appeal SR&ED decision for Bagtech and CCPC status rules in Canada.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Overview of the Dispute and Corporate Context

In Her Majesty the Queen v. Price Waterhouse Coopers Inc., acting in the capacity of Trustee in Bankruptcy of Bioartificial Gel Technologies (Bagtech) Inc. (2013 FCA 164; 2013 CAF 164, affirming 2012 TCC 120), the Federal Court of Appeal ("FCA") issued a landmark judgment governing the intersection of corporate governance architecture and entitlement to enhanced, refundable Scientific Research and Experimental Development ("SR&ED") investment tax credits ("ITCs") under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) ("ITA"). The respondent taxpayer, Bioartificial Gel Technologies (BAGTECH) Inc. ("Bagtech"), was incorporated on April 8, 1996, under the Canada Business Corporations Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-44 ("CBCA"), as a taxable Canadian corporation within the meaning of subsection 89(1) of the ITA, operating in the cutting-edge medical technology sector to develop bioartificial hydrogels. After receiving several rounds of financing over the years, Bagtech assigned its property in 2008, with PricewaterhouseCoopers Inc. ("PwC") appointed as trustee in bankruptcy to prosecute the corporation's disputed SR&ED tax credit refunds before the Tax Court of Canada ("TCC") and the Federal Court of Appeal.

During the taxation years ending December 31, 2004, and December 31, 2005, Bagtech incurred substantial SR&ED current operating expenses and SR&ED capital expenditures within the meaning of subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA. In filing its corporate T2 income tax returns and Form T661 SR&ED schedules for the 2004 and 2005 taxation years, Bagtech claimed status as a "Canadian-controlled private corporation" ("CCPC") pursuant to subsection 125(7) of the ITA. Qualification as a CCPC is the statutory linchpin for early-stage Canadian technology enterprises seeking non-dilutive liquidity from the federal SR&ED program. Whereas non-CCPC corporations are restricted to the basic 20% ITC rate provided for in the definition of "specified percentage" in subsection 127(9), which is generally non-refundable and can only be applied to offset Part I federal income tax otherwise payable, a CCPC may claim an additional 15% credit, for a marked-up total ITC rate of 35%, on its annual expenditure limit (up to $2,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures for the 2004 and 2005 taxation years at issue; the limit was later increased to $3,000,000 and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, to $6,000,000) under subsection 127(10.1) and, crucially, immediate cash refundability of up to 100% of the enhanced credit on current expenditures (and 40% on capital expenditures during the pre-2014 period at issue) under the "refundable investment tax credit" regime in subsections 127.1(1) and 127.1(2) of the ITA.
Capital Structure and the Unanimous Shareholder Agreement

To finance its medical technology research, Bagtech received several rounds of financing over the years, including from European "business angels" and others. As a consequence of these financings, European investors held over 60% of Bagtech's issued and outstanding Class A voting and participating shares during the 2004 and 2005 taxation years (FCA, para. 11). The FCA decision does not identify individual shareholdings, but the European investor group collectively held a clear mathematical majority of the voting shares on the corporate share register throughout both taxation years.

To preserve Canadian governance over the enterprise despite foreign capital dilution, all of Bagtech's shareholders executed a formal agreement in 2003 titled "Unanimous Shareholder Agreement" (the "USA"), which was subsequently amended and re-signed by 100% of the shareholders in 2004 (FCA, para. 12). The USA integrated two critical sets of legal provisions into a single constitutional instrument. First, the agreement contained clauses requiring special shareholder approval for a defined list of corporate management decisions, thereby restricting, in part, the powers of the directors to manage, or supervise the management of, the business and affairs of the corporation in accordance with subsection 146(1) of the CBCA. Second, the agreement contained specific voting clauses governing the election of the board of directors that divided the shareholders into distinct resident and non-resident groups. Pursuant to these director-election clauses, Bagtech's Canadian resident shareholders held the legal right to elect a majority of Bagtech's board of directors throughout the 2004 taxation year and up to July 22, 2005, and thereafter—from July 22, 2005, to December 31, 2005—held the legal right to elect 4 out of 8 directors (50%), ensuring that at no point during the 2004 or 2005 taxation years could the non-resident shareholders elect a majority of the board of directors. The FCA decision does not describe the USA's amendment or termination provisions; it records only that all shareholders signed the Agreement in 2003 and again signed its amended version in 2004.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and Governing Statutory Framework

The Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency ("CRA"), audited Bagtech's 2004 and 2005 claims. As the FCA confirmed, the only issue was whether Bagtech was a CCPC within the meaning of subsection 125(7) of the ITA (para. 5); the decision does not address the scientific or technological eligibility of Bagtech's hydrogel experimentation under the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, or the quantum of its SR&ED operating and capital expenditures, which were not in issue. Instead, the Minister issued Notices of Determination concluding that Bagtech was a non-qualifying corporation entitled to neither the marked-up investment tax credit nor the refundable investment tax credit provided for under subsection 127.1(1).

The statutory dispute turned on the definition of a "Canadian-controlled private corporation" in subsection 125(7) of the ITA, and specifically on the "hypothetical shareholder" aggregation rule in paragraph 125(7)(b). Under subsection 125(7), a CCPC is defined as a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation other than:

items: Under paragraph 125(7)(a), a corporation controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by one or more corporations listed on a designated stock exchange under paragraph 125(7)(c), or by any combination of them; or

Under paragraph 125(7)(b), a corporation that would, if each share of the capital stock of a corporation that is owned by a non-resident person, by a public corporation (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), or by a corporation described in paragraph 125(7)(c) were owned by a single hypothetical "particular person," be controlled by that particular person.

body.text: The parties filed an agreement as to the relevant facts and documents stipulating that if the director-election clauses in Bagtech's USA were excluded from the de jure control analysis under paragraph 125(7)(b), the hypothetical "particular person" (deemed to hold the more than 60% of the Class A voting shares owned by the European investors) would hold de jure control, disqualifying Bagtech from CCPC status. Conversely, if the USA's voting clauses had to be taken into consideration in the de jure control analysis, the hypothetical "particular person" could not elect a majority of the board of directors, and Bagtech qualified as a CCPC entitled to the 35% refundable SR&ED tax credits.

At the Tax Court of Canada, Justice Bédard (2012 TCC 120) allowed Bagtech's appeal, applying the Supreme Court of Canada ("SCC") precedent in Duha Printers (Western) Ltd. v. Canada, [1998] 1 S.C.R. 795, to hold that a USA is a constating document whose limitations on board election rights alter de jure control and bind the hypothetical "particular person" under paragraph 125(7)(b). The Crown appealed the TCC judgment to the Federal Court of Appeal.
The Federal Court of Appeal's Final Holding

In a unanimous judgment delivered at Ottawa on June 21, 2013 (following a hearing in Montréal on April 11, 2013), written by Justice Gauthier and concurred in by Justices Pelletier and Trudel, the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the Crown's appeal with costs and affirmed Bagtech's CCPC status and full entitlement to the enhanced refundable SR&ED tax credits. Reviewing the TCC's decision on the correctness standard applicable to questions of law (Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235), the FCA held that paragraph 85 of Duha Printers conclusively settled that any specific or unique limitation on a majority shareholder's power to control the election of the board of directors manifested in a valid USA must be given full legal effect in determining de jure control. The FCA rejected the Crown's attempt to sever director-election clauses from management-restriction clauses within a CBCA USA, holding that the Judge did not err in law by applying the principles set out at paragraph 85 of Duha Printers (para. 62).
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

While Bagtech's trustee in bankruptcy ultimately prevailed before both the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal, a rigorous legal and technical post-mortem of the decision reveals profound vulnerabilities across two dimensions: first, the taxpayer's corporate and capital-structuring deficiencies that exposed it to a CCPC challenge and to litigation resolved only by the FCA in June 2013, after Bagtech had assigned its property in 2008 (the FCA decision does not attribute the assignment to the tax dispute); and second, the doctrinal and legal failures in the Minister's assessment methodology that the FCA dismantled.
Corporate Governance vs. Substantive SR&ED Eligibility: The "Gatekeeper Disqualification" Trap

In Canadian R&D tax jurisprudence, disputes before the Tax Court of Canada routinely focus on the substantive five-criteria technical test articulated in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839) under subsection 248(1) of the ITA—namely, whether there was a technological uncertainty that could not be resolved by standard practice, whether the taxpayer formulated explicit hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty, whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method including systematic investigation or experimentation, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement, and whether the taxpayer maintained detailed contemporaneous documentation as the work progressed. Alternatively, financial SR&ED disputes typically involve expenditure pool clawbacks for government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) to (20) of the ITA.

In Bagtech, the only issue before the courts was whether Bagtech was a CCPC within the meaning of subsection 125(7) of the ITA (FCA, para. 5); neither the TCC nor the FCA was asked to rule on the eligibility of its bioartificial hydrogel research as SR&ED under subsection 248(1) (a matter typically reviewed by CRA Research and Technology Advisors ("RTAs") and Financial Reviewers) or on its operating and capital expenditure pools under subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9). Nevertheless, Bagtech illustrates that corporate control architecture under subsection 125(7) operates as an unforgiving gatekeeper for SR&ED monetization. For a pre-revenue or clinical-stage technology enterprise with no Part I income tax payable, losing CCPC status does not merely reduce the ITC rate from 35% to 20%; by stripping the corporation of "qualifying corporation" status under subsection 127.1(2), it reduces the immediate cash refund from 100% of the credit to 0%, converting essential working capital into non-refundable tax credit carryforwards trapped inside an illiquid corporate entity. Bagtech's assignment of its property in 2008, four years after its 2004 SR&ED expenses were incurred and five years before the FCA confirmed its CCPC status in 2013, illustrates the practical cost of a prolonged CCPC dispute, although the FCA decision itself does not link the assignment to the tax dispute.
Structural and Contractual Vulnerabilities in Bagtech's Governance Architecture

An examination of the evidentiary record in the TCC (2012 TCC 120) and FCA (2013 FCA 164) exposes four specific corporate and contractual vulnerabilities in Bagtech's setup that triggered the Minister's reassessment and prolonged litigation.
Issuance of Single-Class Voting Equity to Non-Residents Exceeding 50%

The FCA decision records that, during the years at issue, European investors (business angels and others) held over 60% of Bagtech's voting and participating Class A shares (para. 11), and that the director-election rights relied upon were contained in the USA rather than in class-specific voting rights entrenched in the Articles of Incorporation pursuant to subsection 6(1) and subsection 24(4) of the CBCA. With non-resident ownership of Class A shares exceeding 60% in 2004 and 2005, a facial review of Bagtech's Central Securities Register (Share Register) indicated that non-residents held a commanding mathematical majority of the votes attached to the issued share capital. Because CRA financial reviewers routinely verify CCPC status by summing non-resident shareholdings reported on T2 Schedule 19 / Schedule 50 and the Share Register, crossing the 50% threshold on a single voting share class exposed Bagtech to the Minister's determination under paragraph 125(7)(b) that it was a non-qualifying corporation; as the parties agreed, absent the USA's voting clauses Bagtech would not have been a CCPC (FCA, para. 15).
Statutory Tension Between CBCA Section 145.1 (Voting Agreements) and Subsection 146(1) (USAs)

Bagtech relied exclusively on its Unanimous Shareholder Agreement to neutralize the non-residents' more than 60% shareholding. However, the CBCA draws a formal statutory distinction between two different shareholder instruments. Section 145.1 of the CBCA recognizes a written pooling or voting agreement among two or more shareholders governing how they will exercise the voting rights attached to their shares. Under the Supreme Court's decision in Duha Printers, as explained by the FCA (para. 58), director-election clauses contained in a simple private agreement between shareholders (the type of agreement now addressed by section 145.1, to which the provision was moved by the 2001 CBCA amendments, after Duha Printers was decided) are private contractual terms among shareholders, not a constating corporate document, and are not taken into consideration in the de jure control analysis in order to avoid creating uncertainty for taxpayers. Conversely, subsection 146(1) of the CBCA defines a Unanimous Shareholder Agreement as an agreement among all the shareholders of a corporation that "restricts, in whole or in part, the powers of the directors to manage, or supervise the management of, the business and affairs of the corporation".

Unlike the Business Corporations Act (Alberta), R.S.A. 2000, c. B-9 (section 146), which enumerates the matters a USA may address (including the election of directors) and, unlike the CBCA, does not require a USA to restrict the directors' powers in order to qualify as such (FCA, paras. 34 and 60), subsection 146(1) of the CBCA defines a USA solely by reference to restricting the management powers of directors. By embedding its director-election clauses inside a CBCA USA rather than entrenching them as class voting rights in the Articles of Incorporation, Bagtech exposed itself to the Crown's primary legal argument: that the agreement was a "hybrid" document whose director-election clauses did not restrict the directors' powers to manage the business, and therefore operated merely as a severable section 145.1 private voting agreement that must be ignored for tax purposes.
Ordinary Resolution Implementation Mechanics vs. Unanimous Amendment Clauses

The FCA decision does not address any argument based on the USA's ordinary-resolution implementation mechanics; on appeal, the Crown accepted that if the USA's director-election clauses could be considered in the de jure control analysis, the Judge had correctly concluded that Bagtech was a CCPC (FCA, para. 14). When a USA restricts directors' powers by transferring them to the shareholders to be exercised by ordinary (>50%) resolution, a non-resident majority holding more than 60% of the voting shares would directly exercise those transferred management powers, thereby acquiring de jure control through the USA itself. Furthermore, if the USA could be terminated or amended by ordinary resolution or by a standard two-thirds (66.67%) special resolution—which a non-resident block holding more than two-thirds of the votes would meet—the hypothetical "particular person" under paragraph 125(7)(b) would possess the legal power to unilaterally abrogate the USA and elect a new board. The FCA decision does not discuss the USA's amendment or termination clauses; Bagtech prevailed because the FCA held that, under Duha Printers, the USA's director-election clauses had to be taken into consideration, and the Crown accepted that, if so, Bagtech was a CCPC (FCA, paras. 14 and 53).
The Late-2005 50/50 Board Split and De Facto Control Exposure

From July 22, 2005, to December 31, 2005, Bagtech's USA operated such that Canadian resident shareholders elected 4 out of 8 directors (50%); the FCA decision does not specify how the remaining four seats were filled (para. 14). For the purposes of paragraph 125(7)(b), which tests solely de jure control, preventing the non-residents from electing more than 50% (i.e., at least 5 of 8 directors) was legally sufficient to defeat the Minister's assessment because neither group held positive de jure control. However, in broader Canadian tax practice, a 50/50 board deadlock combined with more than 60% non-resident equity ownership creates severe exposure under paragraph 125(7)(a) and subsection 256(5.1) of the ITA, which govern de facto control ("controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever"). Had the Crown adduced evidence and pleaded that a cohesive group of non-resident investors acted in concert to exercise de facto operational or financial control over Bagtech during that 50/50 deadlock period under paragraph 125(7)(a)—rather than relying exclusively on the purely mathematical de jure aggregation rule of paragraph 125(7)(b)—Bagtech's CCPC status could have been jeopardized on factual grounds.
Legal and Doctrinal Failures in the Crown's Position Rejected by the FCA

The Federal Court of Appeal rejected the two arguments advanced by the Crown on appeal (that the Judge interpreted paragraph 85 of Duha Printers too literally and, alternatively, that amendments to the CBCA since 1998 precluded applying it) (paras. 29 to 31); the third issue discussed below was decided by the Tax Court and was not at issue on appeal (para. 17).
Misinterpretation of Paragraph 85 of Duha Printers and the "Severability" Fallacy

Since the Exchequer Court's foundational decision in Buckerfield's Ltd. v. MNR, [1965] 1 Ex. C.R. 299 (64 DTC 5301), "control" of a corporation under the ITA refers to de jure control—the legal right of majority share ownership to elect a majority of the board of directors—unless a statutory provision expressly invokes de facto control ("controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever"). In Duha Printers (Western) Ltd. v. Canada, [1998] 1 S.C.R. 795, Justice Iacobucci synthesized the governing principles of de jure control at paragraph 85, holding that while external private agreements are excluded, a court assessing whether the majority shareholder enjoys "effective control" over the "affairs and fortunes" of the corporation must consider: first, the corporation's governing statute; second, the share register of the corporation; and third, any specific or unique limitation on either the majority shareholder's power to control the election of the board or the board's power to manage the business and affairs of the company, as manifested in either the constating documents of the corporation or any unanimous shareholder agreement.

Before the FCA, the Crown argued that the Tax Court Judge erred in law by interpreting item (3)(c) of paragraph 85 of Duha Printers "too literally". Relying on the Quebec Superior Court decision in Leblanc c. Fertek, REJB 2000-20884, J.E. 2000-2060 (QC C.S.), in which the judge divided a shareholder agreement into two parts (FCA, para. 36), the Crown contended that the court should not let itself be "fooled by the title of the document" signed by Bagtech's shareholders and must divide a CBCA shareholder agreement into two separate parts, treating as a USA under subsection 146(1) only the clauses restricting the directors' management powers while severing and excluding shareholder voting clauses regarding the election of directors.

Justice Gauthier rejected this severability argument as directly contrary to binding Supreme Court of Canada authority. The FCA pointed out that in Duha Printers, the company at issue (Duha No. 2) had been incorporated under the Manitoba Corporations Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. C225, whose relevant USA provisions were modelled on and almost identical to subsection 146(1) of the CBCA. Despite that almost identical statutory text, the Supreme Court in Duha Printers explicitly examined the agreement as a whole and articulated the rule at paragraph 85(3)(c) that a limitation in a USA on "either the majority shareholder's power to control the election of the board or the board's power to manage the business" alters de jure control. Citing Canada v. Craig, 2012 SCC 43, the FCA emphasized, in rejecting the Crown's alternative argument based on amendments to the CBCA since 1998, that only the Supreme Court may modify the rules propounded in its decisions (paras. 54 to 56); separately, the FCA rejected the Crown's narrow reading limiting item (3)(c) to statutes (such as Alberta's) that expressly permit voting clauses in USAs, noting that no authority supported it and that it required adding missing words (paras. 34 to 38). Once an agreement signed by all shareholders restricts the powers of the directors so as to qualify as a USA under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA, the entire agreement forms part of the corporate constitution (the FCA considered Re Systemcorp, (2004), 50 B.L.R. (3d) 163, relied on by Bagtech, and Leblanc c. Fertek, relied on by the Crown, to be of little assistance because neither expressly addressed Duha Printers or de jure control (para. 37)), and its director-election clauses must be given full effect in the de jure control analysis.
Failure to Appreciate the Policy Rationale of Registered Office Accessibility

The FCA also illuminated the policy architecture underlying Duha Printers and the Supreme Court's respect for bona fide legal relationships in tax law. In tax jurisprudence (Shell Canada Ltd. v. Canada, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 622; Duha Printers), courts must respect the legal relationships created by a taxpayer absent a sham or specific statutory recharacterization rule. To balance commercial certainty with an accurate assessment of effective corporate control, the Supreme Court, as explained by the FCA (para. 58), concluded that director-election clauses simply included in private agreements between shareholders should not be taken into consideration, in order to avoid creating uncertainty for taxpayers. By contrast, under subsections 20(1) and 21(2) of the CBCA, a USA is a constating document that must be maintained at the corporation's registered office, where it may be consulted by any representative of the corporation's shareholders or creditors. As Justice Gauthier observed at paragraph 58 of Bagtech, in seeking to strike a fair balance between avoiding uncertainty for taxpayers and recognizing the crucial impact of director-election clauses on effective control, "it is logical that the special nature of USAs, which are constating documents, and the fact that USAs are easily accessible... make a difference. It is not unusual in tax law to obtain a different result by using one form rather than another".
Misapplication of the Two-Stage "Particular Person" Statutory Fiction

At the Tax Court (and underlying the Minister's assessing position), the Crown argued that even if a USA is relevant at the first stage of defining de jure control generally, it must have no influence at the second stage when applying the statutory fiction of the "particular person" under paragraph 125(7)(b), which the Minister contended was "purely arithmetical". The Tax Court rejected this position, holding that the hypothetical shareholder must be considered a party to the Agreement (TCC reasons, paras. 28 to 43); that conclusion was not at issue before the FCA (para. 17). Paragraph 125(7)(b) requires the court to attribute all shares owned by non-residents and public corporations to a single hypothetical "particular person" and then determine whether the corporation would "be controlled by the particular person". Because the hypothetical person steps into the exact legal position attached to those shares under the corporation's constating documents, the hypothetical person is legally bound by the USA to the exact same extent as the actual non-resident shareholders. Because Bagtech's USA prevented the non-resident share block from electing a majority of the board, the hypothetical "particular person" holding more than 60% of the shares could not appoint the majority of Bagtech's directors in 2004 and 2005 (FCA, para. 21).
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in Bagtech against the underlying corporate or administrative failures and the governing legal standard and burden of proof established by the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal.

headers: Taxpayer Structural Vulnerability / Crown Legal Failure
Court's Standard of Proof & Legal Holding

cells: SR&ED Enhanced ITC Rate (35%) & Cash Refundability (100% Current / 40% Capital)
ITA ss. 37(1), 127(9), 127(10.1), 127.1(1), 127.1(2)

Taxpayer Vulnerability: Substantive SR&ED technical eligibility and expenditure quantum were not in issue before the courts (FCA, para. 5), yet 100% of cash refundability and the 15% enhanced ITC mark-up were denied by the Minister and remained in dispute until the FCA's June 21, 2013 judgment, due to foreign equity dilution triggering a CCPC gatekeeper disqualification.

Standard: The facts were agreed by the parties (FCA, para. 8); correctness on the question of law (FCA, para. 28). Holding: The FCA did not rule on the ITC computation; it held only that the Judge did not err in law in applying Duha Printers, leaving intact Bagtech's CCPC status and thus its eligibility for the 35% marked-up and refundable ITCs (paras. 2, 3 and 62).
CCPC Negative Control Threshold (Non-Resident & Public Corp. Exclusion)
ITA s. 125(7) definition of "Canadian-controlled private corporation", paras. (a) and (b)

Taxpayer Vulnerability: Issued single-class (Class A) voting shares to European angel investors totalling over 60% in 2004 and 2005, causing the Share Register to facially fail the 50% arithmetic threshold.

Standard: Statutory compliance with negative conditions in paras. 125(7)(a) and (b). Holding: Majority non-resident voting share ownership (>50%) is not determinative if a valid constating document strips those shares of the power to elect a majority of the board.
The "Hypothetical Particular Person" Aggregation Test
ITA para. 125(7)(b); Duha Printers

Crown Legal Failure: The Minister argued that stage two of the para. 125(7)(b) test is "purely arithmetical" and that the hypothetical "particular person" is not bound by shareholder agreements signed by the actual non-resident shareholders.

Standard: Correctness (question of law). Holding: (Tax Court; not challenged before the FCA, para. 17) The statutory fiction attributes all non-resident and public corporation shares to one hypothetical person, who holds those shares subject to all constating limitations (including a USA).
Test for De Jure Control of a Corporation
Buckerfield's Ltd. v. MNR, 64 DTC 5301; Duha Printers (Western) Ltd. v. Canada, [1998] 1 S.C.R. 795, para. 85

Crown Legal Failure: The Crown argued that item (3)(c) of paragraph 85 of Duha Printers should be read as referring only to restrictions on the directors' powers in a CBCA USA, so that board-election limitations contained in the USA would be disregarded (FCA, paras. 29 to 34).

Standard: Effective control over the affairs and fortunes of the corporation via legal power to elect a majority of the board of directors, determined strictly from (1) the governing statute, (2) the share register, and (3) constating documents including any USA.
Statutory Qualification of a Unanimous Shareholder Agreement (USA)

Taxpayer Vulnerability: If an agreement titled "USA" fails to genuinely restrict the directors' powers to manage the business and affairs of the corporation, or is not signed by 100% of shareholders, it fails to qualify under s. 146(1) CBCA and defaults to an excluded private contract.

Standard: Strict statutory compliance with s. 146(1) CBCA. Holding: Because Bagtech's 2003 and 2004 agreements were signed by all shareholders and restricted the directors' management powers on specified matters, the Agreement qualified as a USA within the meaning of s. 146(1) CBCA, a point that was not disputed (FCA, paras. 12 and 13).
Non-Severability of Voting / Election Clauses Within a Valid CBCA USA
CBCA s. 145.1 vs. s. 146(1); Duha Printers, para. 85(3)(c); Systemcorp A.L.G. Ltd. (Re) and Leblanc c. Fertek (both found of little assistance, FCA para. 37)

Crown Legal Failure: The Crown argued, relying on Leblanc c. Fertek, that director-election clauses inside a CBCA USA do not restrict directors' powers and must be severed as private s. 145.1 pooling agreements excluded from the de jure control analysis.

Standard: Binding vertical stare decisis under Canada v. Craig and Duha Printers. Holding: Once an agreement qualifies as a USA under s. 146(1) CBCA, its provisions cannot be bifurcated; voting clauses governing board elections inside a USA directly govern de jure control.
Board Composition Deadlock (50/50 Split) & Unanimous Amendment Lock

Taxpayer Vulnerability: From July 22 to Dec. 31, 2005, Canadian residents elected 4 of 8 directors (50%). Furthermore, as a general matter not addressed by the FCA, ordinary-resolution clauses in a USA could risk giving a non-resident block holding more than 60% operational control unless locked by a unanimous amendment rule.

Standard: To acquire de jure control under para. 125(7)(b), the hypothetical person must be able to elect a majority (>50%, i.e., at least 5 of 8) of directors or unilaterally repeal the USA. A 50/50 split defeats de jure control by non-residents, though taxpayers must separately guard against de facto control under para. 125(7)(a).

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the appellate principles of Bagtech (2013 FCA 164) into actionable legal and technical tax practice, the following two industry case studies examine realistic Canadian R&D enterprises confronting the exact statutory pitfalls exposed in the ruling. Each case study provides a comprehensive, step-by-step restructuring blueprint across project and corporate governance, contractual terms, technical documentation, and systematic experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Cross-Border Biomaterials & MedTech Venture Facing Foreign VC Majority Dilution and Hybrid USA Vulnerability
Industry Context & Impending Disqualification Pitfalls

NeuroGel BioSystems Inc. ("NeuroGel") is a federally incorporated CBCA corporation based in Montréal, Québec, developing injectable, thermo-responsive bio-hydrogel scaffolds for peripheral nerve regeneration. NeuroGel incurs $2,800,000 annually in qualified SR&ED expenditures—consisting primarily of PhD polymer chemist salaries, preclinical histopathology testing, and specialized rheometer consumables—generating an expected federal refundable SR&ED ITC of $980,000 ($2,800,000 × 35%) alongside Québec R&D tax credits.

To fund Phase I preclinical studies, NeuroGel closes a Series A equity financing led by two European life-sciences venture capital funds and a Boston-based angel syndicate. Following the financing, non-resident investors collectively hold 68% of the voting power via Series A Preferred Shares voting on an as-converted 1:1 basis with Common Shares held by the Canadian founders, who retain 32%. In documenting the transaction, corporate counsel drafted two separate instruments based on US National Venture Capital Association ("NVCA") templates: first, a standalone Voting Agreement under section 145.1 of the CBCA giving the Canadian founders the right to designate 3 of 5 directors and the non-resident VCs the right to designate 2 of 5 directors; and second, a Shareholders' Agreement signed by only 92% of the shareholders (excluding two minor Canadian angel investors) that contains standard investor protective vetoes and states that the agreement may be amended or terminated by the written consent of holders of 66.67% of the voting shares. Simultaneously, one of the European VC portfolio companies, EuroMed GmbH, enters into a "Co-Development and Testing Agreement" paying NeuroGel $450,000 to evaluate specific nerve-conduit hydrogel formulations, while NeuroGel's laboratory team records only final formulation stability pass/fail metrics rather than intermediate polymer cross-linking failures.

Under Bagtech and Duha Printers, NeuroGel faces complete disqualification of its $980,000 refundable federal ITC. Because the Voting Agreement is a standalone section 145.1 CBCA contract containing no restrictions on directors' management powers, and because the Shareholders' Agreement is signed by only 92% of the shareholders (failing the strict 100% unanimity requirement of subsection 146(1) of the CBCA), neither instrument qualifies as a Unanimous Shareholder Agreement. Consequently, both agreements are legally excluded from the de jure control analysis under paragraph 85 of Duha Printers, leaving the hypothetical "particular person" under paragraph 125(7)(b) with 68% voting power and undisputed de jure control. Furthermore, even if the remaining 8% angel shareholders signed the Shareholders' Agreement, the 66.67% amendment clause empowers the hypothetical "particular person" (holding 68%) to unilaterally terminate the agreement and replace the board of directors. Finally, the $450,000 received from EuroMed GmbH risks characterization as non-government assistance or a contract reimbursement under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, reducing the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool, while the lack of failed-iteration logs threatens substantive SR&ED disqualification during the CRA RTA review.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Project and Corporate Governance (CBCA s. 146(1) & ITA s. 125(7))

To secure CCPC status under subsection 125(7) of the ITA and insulate NeuroGel from the type of multi-year CCPC dispute faced by Bagtech, legal counsel must execute a dual-layer constitutional restructuring prior to the commencement of the taxation year (as the additional credit under subsection 127(10.1) is available only to a corporation that was a CCPC throughout the particular taxation year, which is required to preserve the 35% refundable rate). First, counsel must repeal and consolidate the standalone Voting Agreement and the 92%-signed Shareholders' Agreement into a single Unanimous Shareholder Agreement executed by 100% of all Common, Preferred, and non-voting shareholders. To compel the remaining 8% minority angel shareholders to execute the USA, NeuroGel should exercise existing drag-along or compliance covenants or complete a share consolidation/repurchase prior to closing.

Second, to ensure the consolidated instrument qualifies unimpeachably as a statutory USA under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA and cannot be attacked by the CRA as a disguised section 145.1 voting agreement, Article 3 of the USA must incorporate an explicit constitutional provision restricting the powers of the directors to manage, or supervise the management of, the business and affairs of NeuroGel. Specifically, the USA should remove the board's legal authority to approve annual R&D capital budgets exceeding $500,000, incur indebtedness above $250,000, or assign core patent families, transferring those restricted powers to a newly constituted Shareholder Governance Committee composed of a majority of Resident Canadian Shareholders, while expressly stating pursuant to subsection 146(5) of the CBCA that the directors are relieved of their duties and liabilities to the extent their powers are so restricted.

Third, the director nomination, election, and removal provisions must be embedded directly inside Article 4 of the USA, stipulating that the board of directors consists of 5 directors, of whom 3 directors (60%) are nominated and elected exclusively by the Resident Canadian Shareholders, and 2 directors (40%) are nominated and elected by the Non-Resident Shareholders. Crucially, the USA must override subsection 109(1) of the CBCA (as permitted by subsection 146(1) and subsection 6(3) of the CBCA) by stipulating that a director elected by the Resident Canadian Shareholders may only be removed or replaced by the Resident Canadian Shareholders, and that the 66.67% amendment clause is replaced by an absolute 100% Unanimity Requirement for any amendment, waiver, or termination of the USA. Under Bagtech, this guarantees that when the CRA aggregates the 68% non-resident shareholdings into the hands of the hypothetical "particular person" under paragraph 125(7)(b), that hypothetical shareholder is bound by the USA and lacks the legal power either to elect a majority of the board or to repeal the USA. To eliminate any administrative delay during initial CRA desk audits, NeuroGel should simultaneously file Articles of Amendment under section 173 and subsection 24(4) of the CBCA entrenching those exact class-specific director election rights (3 of 5 directors elected by Class A Resident Shares; 2 of 5 directors elected by Class B Non-Resident Preferred Shares) directly in the Articles of Incorporation.
Step 2: Restructuring Commercial and R&D Contract Terms (ITA ss. 37(1) & 127(9))

To prevent the $450,000 payment from EuroMed GmbH from eroding NeuroGel's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool, counsel must restructure the commercial arrangement before execution. Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, a payment from a foreign corporation not carrying on business in Canada is generally not a "contract payment" (which applies to taxable Canadian suppliers), but it will still reduce the SR&ED expenditure pool if it constitutes "non-government assistance"—defined in subsection 127(9) to include any reimbursement, grant, subsidy, or inducement in respect of the R&D expenses—or if the contract strips NeuroGel of the requirement under subsection 37(1) that the SR&ED be undertaken "by or on behalf of the taxpayer" and related to a business of the taxpayer.

Counsel must therefore replace the "Co-Development and Testing Agreement" with an arm's-length Commercial Option and Non-Exclusive Field-of-Use Licence Agreement. The redrafted contract must stipulate that NeuroGel retains 100% legal and beneficial ownership of all background and foreground intellectual property, polymer formulations, and experimental data; that NeuroGel bears 100% of the financial and technical risk of experimental failure with zero obligation to reimburse expenses or deliver a successful product; and that the $450,000 constitutes non-refundable commercial option consideration granting EuroMed GmbH a time-limited right of first negotiation for a European distribution licence if and only if NeuroGel's internal R&D program achieves commercial viability.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Experimentation Tracking (ITA s. 248(1) & Form T661)

To ensure rapid approval by the CRA RTA once CCPC status is confirmed, NeuroGel's technical leadership must restructure its laboratory documentation around the five criteria of Northwest Hydraulic Consultants. In Part 2 of Form T661 (Line 242), NeuroGel must articulate the specific technological uncertainty by demonstrating why standard poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and hyaluronic acid cross-linking ratios known in the public domain fail to achieve the simultaneous mechanical shear-thinning viscosity (during 27-gauge micro-needle injection) and post-injection storage modulus (of at least 1 kPa at 37°C within 45 seconds) required to prevent axonal die-back without inducing cytotoxic free-radical generation.

In Line 244 of Form T661 and in the underlying Electronic Laboratory Notebooks ("ELNs"), polymer chemists must record each experimental cycle sequentially using a structured Hypothesis-Test-Analysis protocol. Each entry must log the specific stoichiometric modification of thiol-Michael addition cross-linkers hypothesized to decouple gelation kinetics from network stiffness, followed by quantitative rheometric oscillation time-sweeps, swelling ratio measurements, and dorsal root ganglia viability assays that explicitly preserve failed experimental batches (such as premature syringe occlusion or hydrolytic scaffold collapse at Day 14). Finally, NeuroGel must implement weekly time-tracking sheets that link each researcher's payroll hours directly to specific ELN Hypothesis IDs, segregating eligible experimental development under subsection 248(1) from excluded routine quality control or regulatory dossier formatting.

ITA s. 248(1) ("SR&ED"); Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen.

body.text: Case Study 2: Publicly Backed Canadian AI & Quantum Semiconductor Enterprise Facing Combined Public Corporation & Non-Resident Aggregation Under Paragraph 125(7)(b)
Industry Context & Impending Disqualification Pitfalls

Q-Silicon Photonics Corp. ("Q-Silicon") is a CBCA-incorporated deep-tech hardware and software enterprise headquartered in Waterloo, Ontario, developing fault-tolerant cryogenic CMOS controller integrated circuits and machine-learning error-mitigation compilers for photonic quantum processors. Q-Silicon incurs $3,000,000 in qualified SR&ED salary and subcontractor expenditures during its current taxation year, targeting a $1,050,000 refundable federal ITC ($3,000,000 × 35%) under subsections 127(10.1) and 127.1(1) of the ITA, as well as the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit ("OITC") on qualified expenditures for SR&ED carried on in Ontario.

Q-Silicon's issued share capital consists of a single class of Common Shares distributed across three shareholder groups: Canadian Founders & Employees (private individuals resident in Canada) holding 44% of the voting shares; OmniTel Corp. (a Canadian public corporation listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange) holding 31% of the voting shares; and PacRim Semiconductor Inc. (a Delaware, USA non-resident corporation) holding 25% of the voting shares. All shareholders have executed a valid Unanimous Shareholder Agreement under subsection 146(1) of the CBCA restricting the directors' powers to manage the corporation. Under the board composition clause of the USA, the board consists of 6 directors: 3 directors nominated and elected by the Canadian Founders, 2 directors nominated and elected by OmniTel Corp., and 1 director nominated and elected by PacRim Semiconductor Inc.—creating a 3-to-3 (50/50) split between Canadian private residents and the institutional investors. However, the USA and corporate By-laws stipulate that in the event of a tie vote on the board, the Chair of the Board (who is appointed by OmniTel Corp. as the largest institutional shareholder) holds a casting (tie-breaking) vote. Additionally, OmniTel Corp. holds a convertible promissory note exercisable at any time into an additional 10% of Q-Silicon's shares, and Q-Silicon subcontracts $400,000 of cryogenic wafer characterization testing to a university laboratory in Massachusetts.
Under Bagtech and the statutory framework of the ITA, Q-Silicon faces three severe disqualifications:

items: Paragraph 125(7)(b) Combined Aggregation of Public Corporations and Non-Residents: Corporate advisors frequently overlook that paragraph 125(7)(b) does not test non-resident ownership and public corporation ownership in isolation. As set out in paragraph 125(7)(b) of the ITA and examined in Bagtech, the statute aggregates into the single hypothetical "particular person" each share owned by a non-resident person OR by a public corporation. Consequently, the hypothetical "particular person" is deemed to own 56% of Q-Silicon's voting shares (31% owned by TSX-listed OmniTel Corp. plus 25% owned by US-resident PacRim Semiconductor Inc.).

Defeat of the 50/50 Board Split by the Chair's Casting Vote and Paragraph 251(5)(b): While Bagtech survived a 4-of-8 (50/50) board split during the second half of 2005 because the non-residents could not elect more than 50% of the board, Q-Silicon's USA grants the Chair (appointed by TSX-listed OmniTel Corp.) a legal casting vote. Under Canadian de jure control jurisprudence (Buckerfield's; Duha Printers), holding 50% of the board seats combined with a legal tie-breaking casting vote confers positive de jure control on the hypothetical "particular person" under paragraph 125(7)(b), immediately destroying Q-Silicon's CCPC status. Furthermore, OmniTel's convertible note triggers paragraph 251(5)(b) of the ITA, which deems a person holding a contractual right (immediately or in the future and whether absolutely or contingently) to acquire shares or control voting rights to be in the same position in relation to control as if that person owned the shares at that time.

Foreign Subcontractor Expenditure Exclusion (ITA s. 37(1) & s. 37(2)): The $400,000 paid to the Massachusetts university laboratory is for SR&ED performed outside Canada; under subsection 37(2) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, third-party subcontracted research performed outside Canada cannot be included in the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool for ITC purposes.

body.text: Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Project and Corporate Governance (USA Board Mechanics & ITA para. 251(5)(b))

To restore CCPC status and protect the $1,050,000 federal refundable ITC and 8% OITC, Q-Silicon must immediately amend its Unanimous Shareholder Agreement with 100% shareholder execution. First, counsel must eliminate the 50/50 board split and abolish the Chair's casting vote. The amended USA should expand the board from 6 to 7 directors, granting the Canadian Founders & Resident Private Shareholders the exclusive legal right to nominate, elect, remove, and replace 4 of the 7 directors (57.14%), while TSX-listed OmniTel Corp. elects 2 directors and US-resident PacRim Semiconductor Inc. elects 1 director. Both the USA and the corporate By-laws must be amended to explicitly abolish any casting or tie-breaking vote for the Chair of the Board, and to require that a quorum for any board meeting include at least 3 directors elected by the Canadian Resident Private Shareholders.

Second, to fortify the CBCA subsection 146(1) constitutional validity of the USA under Justice Gauthier's reasoning in Bagtech (paragraphs 32 to 58), the USA must maintain substantive restrictions on the board's management powers—such as transferring authority over annual R&D budgets, IP licensing, and executive appointments to the shareholders—while subjecting those transferred powers to a Dual-Group Shareholder Approval Mechanism requiring both (i) an ordinary majority vote of the Canadian Resident Private Shareholders and (ii) an ordinary majority vote of all shareholders. This prevents the Crown from arguing (an argument the FCA decision in Bagtech does not address) that transferred management powers exercisable by simple shareholder resolution allow the 56% public/non-resident block to control the company directly.

Third, counsel must neutralize the paragraph 251(5)(b) trap created by OmniTel Corp.'s convertible promissory note. The convertible note and the USA must be amended so that upon conversion, the note converts strictly into Class B Non-Voting Participating Preferred Shares (or into shares bound by the USA's fixed 2-of-7 director cap for OmniTel Corp.), accompanied by an explicit "CCPC Preservation Override Clause" in the USA stating that no share issuance, conversion, option exercise, or proxy shall confer any right to alter the Canadian Resident Private Shareholders' exclusive right to elect at least 4 of the 7 directors, and that the USA may only be amended or terminated by 100% unanimous consent of all shareholders. Finally, in strict compliance with subsections 20(1), 21(2), and 49(8) of the CBCA (the first two of which the FCA in Bagtech highlighted at paragraph 58 as the policy justification for treating a USA as a constating document), Q-Silicon must legend all share certificates with a conspicuous reference to the USA and lodge the executed USA in the corporate minute book at its registered office in Waterloo.
Step 2: Restructuring Subcontractor and Strategic Partner Contracts (ITA ss. 37(1), 37(2) & 127(9))

To recover the tax credit eligibility of the $400,000 cryogenic wafer testing expenditure and insulate Q-Silicon from non-arm's-length assistance adjustments with OmniTel Corp., Q-Silicon must restructure its external R&D contracts. Because third-party contract payments for work performed outside Canada are ineligible for SR&ED ITCs under subsections 37(1), 37(2), and 127(9) of the ITA, Q-Silicon must terminate the Massachusetts testing subcontract for subsequent fabrication cycles and onshore the cryogenic characterization work to an arm's-length Canadian university nanofabrication facility or a taxable Canadian testing laboratory performing the work physically within Ontario (qualifying 80% of the arm's-length contract payment for the 35% federal ITC and 8% OITC). Alternatively, where specialized dilution refrigerators are leased at a Canadian research institute and operated directly by Q-Silicon's own salaried quantum engineers, 100% of the allocable Canadian employee salaries qualify under paragraph 37(1)(a) and subsection 127(9). With respect to OmniTel Corp.'s cloud compute cluster, Q-Silicon must execute an arm's-length commercial Master Services Agreement billed at standard market rates so that compute access cannot be characterized by the CRA as non-government assistance or a shareholder benefit under subsection 127(9).
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Experimentation Tracking for Hardware/Software SR&ED

To substantiate the $3,000,000 SR&ED expenditure claim across Q-Silicon's hybrid semiconductor and quantum-compiler development environment, technical advisors must structure the Form T661 filing into two distinct SR&ED projects that separate fundamental system-level technological uncertainties from routine engineering. The first project, Cryogenic CMOS Thermal-Dissipation & Charge-Noise Suppression, must document the technological uncertainty arising from the physical breakdown of standard BSIM MOSFET foundry models below 4 K, where carrier freeze-out, kink effects, and flicker noise invalidate standard circuit simulation parameters and prevent deterministic impedance matching with photonic qubits. The second project, Real-Time Quantum Error-Mitigation Compiler Architecture, must document the algorithmic uncertainty of achieving sub-microsecond decoding latency for surface-code syndrome extraction under non-Markovian hardware noise profiles.

To generate an audit-proof contemporaneous evidentiary trail satisfying Northwest Hydraulic Consultants, Q-Silicon must configure its Git version-control repositories, Jira engineering tickets, and silicon simulation logs so that every experimental branch is tagged with a mandatory SRED-HYP-[Number] identifier tied to a formulated technical hypothesis. Hardware and software engineers must log SPICE cryogenic simulation divergences, cryo-prober waveform anomalies, and compiler latency bottlenecks directly in commit messages and bi-weekly sprint retrospectives, linking bi-weekly payroll hours to those exact hypothesis tags. Combined with the Bagtech-compliant CBCA Unanimous Shareholder Agreement, this integrated legal and technical governance framework guarantees both substantive SR&ED eligibility and undisputed CCPC entitlement to the 35% federal and 8% provincial refundable tax credits.

ITA ss. 37(1), 37(2), 127(9), 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Consultants.
